newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel fails to convince Egypt on Jerusalem housing.
newsitem.headline: Israel fails to convince Egypt on Jerusalem housing.

text.p: Israel failed to convince Egypt of its good intentions in Arab East Jerusalem on Wednesday and Egypt refused to set free an Israeli man accused of spying.

But Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, speaking after talks with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, did say he wanted to lower the temperature in the row over Israeli plans to build more houses for Jews in the disputed part of the city.
Netanyahu defended the decision to build 6,500 houses in the Jabal Abu Ghneim quarter, saying Jerusalem was desperately short of housing for both Jews and Arabs.
He also said Palestinians were free to live in any part of the city -- a claim Palestinians say is completely baseless.

Answering Netanyahu's long attempt to justify the housing project, Mubarak told a joint news conference: "I cannot tell you I'm convinced. I'm afraid this will create problems in future and I have to look at this again... I'm going to see to it with Mr Arafat, who will be coming tomorrow at night."
"We are not thinking of taking measures (against Israel). Our measures are to push the peace process forward on a fair basis to be a lasting peace," he added.

Yasser Arafat, the Palestinian leader, will be on his way back from the United States, where he discussed the Jerusalem housing project with U.S. President Bill Clinton, who said it created "mistrust".

Mubarak, known for his cool temperament, showed no sign of the exasperation with Israeli policy evident in the Egyptian press. "I know that the Jerusalem issue is a very warm issue now but I hope it can be solved in a convenient way to both sides and not to create problems and lower the tone now," he said.
On the related dispute over an Israeli order that four Palestinian offices close down in East Jerusalem, Netanyahu offered the Palestinians a few days to make a legal challenge.
The Israeli government says the Palestinian Authority (PA) has been running the offices in violation of the Oslo peace agreement, which banned PA activity in the city.

"It would take several days for the (closure) notices to be acted upon. During these days the Palestinians can appeal to our court and argue we are wrong... If they succeed in convincing the court, they will remain open," Netanyahu said.
The prime minister also brought up other Israeli grievances against Palestinian compliance with the Oslo agreements.

"We'd like the complete revision of the Palestinian charter, we'd like to see action against terrorists who are involved in some of worst outrages against Israel. They shouldn't be roaming around free, they should be put in jail. We'd like to see the collection of illegal weapons," he said.

Netanyahu had said that his priority in his talks with Mubarak would be to secure the release of Azam Azam, an Israeli technician detained in November and accused of spying in Egypt for the Israeli secret service Mossad.

Asked if he would set Azam free, Mubarak said: "This case is before the court. We have no authority to exclude it from the court until it comes to an end. Before that we are not authorised, even our constitution doesn't give us the right to do anything or to release him."
Netanyahu stood to Mubarak's side but did not comment on the espionage case throughout the news conference.

But late on Tuesday he said: "Azam Azam is at the top of my agenda... He has been jailed on a false charge of espionage... He is not an agent of any of the Israeli intelligence organs -- I can guarantee that... He is an Israeli citizen who has been falsely accused and we want him out."
The visit was Netanyahu's second to Egypt since he took office last June and his first since Israel and the Palestinians signed an agreement on the West bank town of Hebron in January.
After Netanyahu's first visit, Mubarak said he had reneged on promises he made in their talks and he refused to see him again until he made a deal on Hebron.
Asked if he now trusted the Israeli leader, Mubarak said: "I didn't mean I didn't trust Mr Netanyahu as a man. Sometimes I felt there was no implementation of the previous agreement."
